run.request: We want to redo our small galley kitchen for $25,000 or less. We are keeping the layout, but want new cabinets, counters, a backsplash and appliances. Where should the money go, what order do we do things in, and what usually goes wrong?
run.title: Your galley kitchen remodel for $25,000 or less: budget, order of work and common problems
run.goal: You can split a $25,000 budget across cabinets, counters, backsplash and appliances, schedule the work in the right order, and avoid the problems that most often push galley remodels over budget.
run.summary: Put the most money into cabinets (about $7,000) and appliances (about $4,500). Hold $3,500 back as contingency, and save on counters and tile with laminate, butcher block or plain ceramic subway tile. Order and receive the cabinets and appliances before anyone tears anything out. Then follow this order: cabinets, counter templating, counters, sink, backsplash. Most overruns come from hidden water damage, uneven walls and floors, wrong appliance sizes and changes made mid-job, and each one has a simple check you can do first.

sections.heading: Where the $25,000 goes

body.text: Plan with the target column, not the ranges. The targets add up to exactly $25,000, and $3,500 of that (14 percent) is set aside as contingency. All figures are 2026 mid-range estimates for a 70 to 100 square foot galley with 15 to 22 linear feet of cabinets. The ranges show what each line can cost. If one line comes in near the top of its range, take the difference from another line, not from the contingency.

items: Cabinets: stock or ready-to-assemble (RTA) boxes cost roughly 30 to 50 percent less than semi-custom, an estimate. A galley uses standard widths, so custom sizes rarely pay off.
Counters: laminate or butcher block saves an estimate of $1,000 to $2,000 compared with quartz on every run. Installed prices are in the counter table in the next section.
Appliances: a standard 30 inch range and a freestanding fridge cost far less than built-in or panel-ready models. A matching four-piece package often comes with a 10 to 20 percent bundle discount.
Backsplash: plain ceramic subway tile at $5 to $15 per square foot looks clean and keeps labor simple. Patterned or handmade tile costs much more to buy and install.
Drawer boxes and slides: pay for solid wood or metal boxes with full-extension, soft-close slides. Expect about $300 to $800 more, an estimate. Drawers wear out first in a busy galley.
Hinges: soft-close hinges from a known brand add little cost and stop doors from sagging.

The main prep counter: if you mix materials, put quartz or solid stone on the run where you chop and plate, and laminate or butcher block on the other side. You get a durable surface where it matters for about half the price of stone everywhere.
Sink and faucet: a deep single-bowl sink and a pull-down faucet with metal valves cost about $200 to $400 more than builder-grade, an estimate, and they last much longer.

body.text: Flooring is not in this budget. If you need new flooring, plan on about $1,000 to $2,500 (an estimate) and take it from cabinets or appliances first. Leave the contingency alone until the walls are open.

rows: Stock or semi-stock boxes, doors, hardware
Fridge, range, hood or microwave, dishwasher
Cabinet install, hookups, patch and paint

revised: The counter prices don't match the choices table. Change laminate from "$25 to $50" to "$25 to $60" per square foot installed, and butcher block from "$40 to $80" to "$40 to $100".
Mark the savings figures as estimates. Write "an estimate of $1,000 to $2,000" for the laminate or butcher block savings, and "roughly 30 to 50 percent less, an estimate" for the cabinet savings.
The two bullet lists have no labels. Add a short sentence before each one, such as "Save money here:" and "Spend more here:", so the reader can tell them apart.

sections.heading: Picking cabinets, counters, backsplash and appliances for a galley

body.text: A galley works when every inch is planned. Measure the room before you choose anything: the full length of each wall, the aisle width from counter edge to counter edge, and where windows, doors and outlets sit. With 15 to 22 linear feet of cabinets, you have roughly 30 to 45 square feet of counter and 25 to 40 square feet of backsplash wall. Use those numbers when you price materials.

items: Stock cabinets come in fixed widths, usually in 3 inch steps. They ship fast and cost the least. Gaps get covered with filler strips, so plan for 1 to 3 inches of filler at each wall end.
RTA cabinets arrive flat packed. Many use plywood boxes for less money than stock. You or the installer assemble them, which adds labor time.
Semi-custom cabinets offer more widths, depths and finishes. They help when a wall is an odd length. Expect longer lead times.
In any grade, choose plywood boxes if you can, and drawers instead of doors in the lower cabinets. Drawers are easier to reach in a narrow room than deep shelves.
Run upper cabinets to the ceiling, or add a short stacked cabinet on top. A galley has little wall space, so the extra storage counts.
Aisle: keep at least 42 inches between counters for one cook and 48 inches for two. 36 inches is the bare minimum and feels tight once a dishwasher or oven door is open.
Do not put the dishwasher directly across from the oven or the fridge. An open dishwasher door sticks out about 24 to 27 inches and blocks the aisle. Offset them by at least one cabinet width.
Put the fridge at the end of a run with its hinge side toward the wall, so the door opens back out of the way.
Leave landing space: about 15 inches of counter beside the fridge handle, 12 to 15 inches on each side of the range, and 18 to 24 inches beside the sink.
Use fillers where drawers meet a wall or a door frame, so handles do not hit.
Range: 30 inches is standard and fits most galleys. A 24 inch range saves 6 inches of counter for prep but limits pot size.
Fridge: standard-depth fridges stick out 5 to 8 inches past the counter. A counter-depth model, about 24 to 25 inches deep without doors, keeps the aisle clear. Widths run 24, 30, 33 or 36 inches.
Dishwasher: 24 inches is standard. An 18 inch model works for one or two people and frees space for a drawer stack.
Hood: vent it outside if you can, and match the range width or go 3 inches wider. An over-the-range microwave saves upper space but vents poorly.
Lock in exact appliance models and their spec sheets before the cabinet order. Cabinet openings are sized to them.

body.text: For the backsplash, light and glossy tile makes a narrow room feel wider. Ceramic subway tile (3 by 6 or 3 by 12 inches) is cheap and easy to set. Porcelain resists stains. Glass mosaic looks sharp but costs more to install. A simple option is to run your counter material 4 inches up the wall and paint above it. Tile material alone runs about $3 to $30 per square foot, an estimate, before labor.

revised: "Seamless" is a banned buzzword. In the counter table's solid surface row, change "Seamless look" to "No visible seams".

sections.heading: The order to do things in

body.text: Plan the job in two phases. The first phase is planning and ordering, and your kitchen still works during it. The second phase starts with demolition, and from then on you have no working kitchen. Keep that second phase as short as possible. Do not tear anything out until your cabinets and appliances are in your house.

Some steps can't start until another one is finished. Counters can't be measured until the cabinets are installed and level. The sink can't be hooked up until the counter is in. The backsplash goes in after the counter, so the tile sits on the finished surface. Inspections can also hold up the next step. Book each inspector as soon as the work is ready, and don't close up walls until the rough inspection passes.

Total timeline (estimate): 10 to 20 weeks from first measurements to final sign-off. Of that, expect to be without a working kitchen for about 4 to 8 weeks. The longest wait is usually between cabinet install and counter install.

items: Set up a temporary kitchen in another room before demolition day. Include the old fridge if it still works, plus a microwave, a toaster oven or air fryer, an electric kettle and a slow cooker or multicooker.
Wash dishes in a laundry sink or bathtub, or use reusable plastic tubs. Keep a small stock of paper plates for the busiest weeks.
Plan simple meals a week at a time, and cook and freeze a few dinners before demolition starts.
Ask your contractor to seal off the kitchen with plastic sheeting and zip doors. Cover air vents so dust stays out of the rest of the house.
Clear a dry spot in the garage or another room for deliveries.

sections.heading: What usually goes wrong and how to prevent it

body.text: Most galley remodels go over budget for a few common reasons. The table lists them from most to least common. Each row gives the warning sign to look for, how to prevent it, and an estimated cost if it happens anyway. All costs are rough 2026 US ranges.

items: Before demolition, open the sink cabinet and press on the floor with a screwdriver. Soft wood, dark stains or a musty smell mean you have a leak to fix first.
Before you order anything, measure the walls in three places, check the corners with a framing square and lay a 6 foot level on the floor. Give those numbers to your cabinet supplier.
Unbox and inspect every cabinet and appliance the day it arrives. Photograph any damage and report it before you sign the delivery slip.
Write down every change after work starts, with its price, and sign it before the work is done.

body.text: Call a licensed electrician for any new circuit, panel work, or moved or added outlet. Also call one if you see two-prong outlets, cloth-covered or aluminum wire, outlets that feel warm, or breakers that trip often. Call a licensed plumber if a shutoff valve will not close fully, if you find old galvanized pipe, if you need to move a drain, or for any gas range hookup. In most areas this work needs a permit, and only the licensed trade can pull it.

Your $3,500 contingency is there to cover these costs. Do not spend it on upgrades until the cabinets and counters are in. By then most of the hidden problems will have shown up. Only joist repair or a panel upgrade, at $1,500 to $4,000 each, is likely to use up most or all of it alone.

next_steps: Measure the room: wall lengths in three places, corner squareness, floor level and aisle width. Probe the floor under the sink for soft spots.
Have an electrician check your circuits and panel, then pick exact appliance models and save their spec sheets.
Choose cabinets and counter materials using the planning targets, and confirm aisle clearances and door swings on the layout.
Order cabinets and appliances, get confirmed delivery dates and apply for permits while you wait.
Set up a temporary kitchen, and start demolition only after every cabinet and appliance has arrived and been checked.
assumptions: The kitchen is about 70 to 100 square feet with roughly 15 to 22 linear feet of cabinets, in the US, at mid-range 2026 prices.
Plumbing, gas and electrical stay where they are, apart from small changes like new outlets or under-cabinet lights.
You hire a general contractor or separate trades for most of the work and do little of it yourself.
The $25,000 covers everything, including labor, permits, delivery and a $3,500 contingency.
Flooring is not included. New flooring would add about $1,000 to $2,500, an estimate.
checks: The budget lines add up to $25,000 or less and include a contingency of at least 10 percent.
Every price and duration is marked as an estimate and given as a range.
The work order puts cabinet install before counter templating, and counter install before backsplash and the sink hookup.
Galley-specific clearances such as aisle width and facing doors are addressed, and the layout stays unchanged.
Each common problem has a prevention step, not only a description.
conflicts: Laminate counters: the budget part says $25 to $50 per sq ft installed, and the choices table says $25 to $60.
Butcher block counters: the budget part says $40 to $80 per sq ft installed, and the choices table says $40 to $100.
